title: Silent female representation and tech entrepreneurial project evaluation: The role of evaluators' genders
authors: Yan “Anthea” Zhang; Lun Li; Jizhen Li; Xiwei Yi
affiliations: School of Business Rice University Houston Texas USA; Business School Beijing Normal University Beijing China; School of Economics and Management Tsinghua University Beijing China; Guanghua School of Management Peking University Beijing China
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We examine how the nature of female representation in tech entrepreneurial projects may be related to the evaluations of the projects. We argue that silent female representation —i.e., women are present but do not speak in representing projects—may reinforce the stereotyped view of women, resulting in lower project evaluations relative to male‐only projects, whereas active female representation may not lead to evaluation penalty. We further predict that the negative association between silent female representation and project evaluation is stronger when the evaluators are women than when they are men. Conducted in a unique setting wherein female and male evaluators on panels, independently and confidentially, rated funding applications represented by various mixes of male and female entrepreneurs, our study provides evidence that is consistent with these predictions. Managerial Summary It is widely recognized that female entrepreneurs face greater challenges than their male counterparts when seeking external financial resources in the tech sector. This funding disparity may start from evaluation disparity. We find that projects with silent female representation—i.e., women are present but do not speak—receive lower evaluations than male‐only projects, whereas projects with active female representation receive evaluations comparable to male‐only projects. We also find that female evaluators are more likely than male evaluators to penalize projects with silent female representation. Our research offers valuable insights into strategies for fostering gender equality in traditionally male‐dominated fields.

title: Should birds of a feather flock together: How public criticism shapes pressures for sustainability conformity and differentiation
authors: Nareuporn (Bell) Piyasinchai; Matthew Grimes
affiliations: Department of Organization Studies Tilburg University Tilburg the Netherlands; Cambridge Judge Business School University of Cambridge Cambridge UK
abstract: Abstract Research Summary While firms face pressure to engage in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) practices, it is unclear how they should specifically engage given the breadth of sustainability‐related concerns. Drawing on optimal distinctiveness and social evaluations research, we argue that public criticism directed toward an industry creates oscillating pressures for firms to conform with or deviate from industry ESG norms. Using data on 8176 global companies from 2013 to 2022, we find that although ESG conformity benefits investor evaluations, once industry peers' public criticism accumulates beyond a threshold, ESG differentiation is rewarded, particularly when firms increase material ESG practices and reduce immaterial ones. Our study reveals how public criticism dynamically reshapes the evaluative processes by which investors determine firm legitimacy, bridging optimal distinctiveness and social evaluations literatures. Managerial Summary Our research indicates that firms often adopt similar ESG practices as their industry peers, which usually enhances investor evaluations. However, this conformity can backfire and become a liability when industry peers face significant criticism. In such scenarios, firms that adopt distinctive ESG practices compared to the industry tend to receive greater rewards, especially when differentiation involves increasing material ESG practices and reducing immaterial ones. Therefore, while adopting ESG norms can be beneficial, managers should be vigilant of public opinion and ready to deviate from those norms when necessary.

title: Influence Without Authority: Bottom-Up Normalization of Organizational Corruption
authors: Patricia Helena Hein; Shahzad (Shaz) Ansari
affiliations: Western University, Ivey Business School, London, Canada; University of Cambridge, Judge Business School, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
abstract: Research on organizational corruption has largely portrayed normalization as a top-down, management-driven process. We know less about how employees with limited formal authority can escalate wrongdoing beyond isolated acts and drive its normalization. Drawing on a qualitative study of a German recruitment firm’s practices during the COVID-19 pandemic, we develop a three-phase model of bottom-up normalization of organizational wrongdoing. Less powerful actors first engage in tolerated rule-bending to demonstrate competence and indispensability and build influence through informal networks. When disruption threatens this influence and legitimate alternatives are unavailable, they may escalate to more serious wrongdoing to safeguard their standing by framing new opportunities as extensions of familiar rule-bending. Normalization then depends on their ability to sustain a cohesive coalition, secure support from actors with formal authority, and contain resistance. We make three contributions. First, we advance a relational view of corruption by showing how central positions in informal networks enable actors lacking formal authority to mobilize support across hierarchical levels and normalize wrongdoing. Second, we show how organizational corruption can become a means of building and preserving social influence, fostering a sense of accomplishment rather than guilt or shame. Third, we identify a disruption-driven pathway to normalization in which threats to less powerful actors’ social influence precipitate abrupt escalation from tolerated rule-bending to more serious wrongdoing.

title: Opinion Trumps Fact: Entry and Competition in Online Political News
authors: Aaron Chatterji; Sharique Hasan; William D. Miles; Dror Shvadron
affiliations: Fuqua School of Business, Duke University, Durham, North Carolina 27708; and NBER, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138; Fuqua School of Business, Duke University, Durham, North Carolina 27708; Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 3E6, Canada
abstract: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021. Using a novel measure of article opinionation that captures the extent to which an article displays editorializing and persuasive language, we provide correlational evidence that new entrants produce articles that are more opinionated than those of incumbents, even when reporting on the same event. We then show that there is an economic rationale for this content strategy: opinionated articles receive more engagement on Twitter, and this engagement translates to increased webpage visits, crucial for advertising revenue. Consistent with these incentives, we provide evidence that news providers increase the average opinion level in their articles in response to competition and advertiser pressure. These shifts are accompanied by a possibly unintended consequence: opinionated content is associated with greater anger and hate speech in social media engagement. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01487 .

title: Corporate Contributions to Ballot Measure Campaigns: Real Effects and Valuation
authors: Rüdiger Fahlenbrach; Alexei Ovtchinnikov; Philip Valta
affiliations: Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, 1015 Lausanne, Switzerland; and Swiss Finance Institute, 8006 Zürich, Switzerland; and European Corporate Governance Institute, 1000 Brussels, Belgium; HEC Paris, 78350 Jouy-en-Josas, France; University of Bern, 3012 Bern, Switzerland
abstract: We analyze novel data on corporate contributions to ballot initiatives at the U.S. state level. Firms make large contributions to ballot measure campaigns in favor of or against specific initiatives. They contribute significantly more to business initiatives compared with ideological initiatives. Corporate campaign spending is systematically associated with the likelihood that a ballot measure passes. Contributing firms experience changes in sales growth following the passage of important ballot measures. Following successful (failed) initiatives, all firms in affected industries exhibit significantly more positive (negative) cumulative abnormal returns around the election, but contributing firms do more so than peers. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: R. Fahlenbrach gratefully acknowledges financial support from the Swiss Finance Institute. title: Does Feedback Enhance Diversity in Selection Decisions?
authors: Jose A. Cervantez; Sophia L. Pink; Linda W. Chang; Aneesh Rai; Katherine L. Milkman
affiliations: The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104; Robert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland 20742
abstract: Some organizations provide employees with feedback on the demographics of people they have chosen to spotlight, hire, and promote, hoping to spur more diverse future selections. However, it is an open question whether purely descriptive feedback accomplishes this. We theorize and show that descriptive feedback highlighting low past selection rates of women or racial minorities (e.g., “5% of previous experts interviewed were women”) triggers a motivation to respond without prejudice, increasing the subsequent selection of members of underrepresented groups. Conversely, providing descriptive feedback about low selection rates of people with other attributes (e.g., areas of expertise, geographical location) that do not evoke image or reputational concerns has less influence on future decisions. We demonstrate these patterns across seven preregistered experiments (total n = 6,502), including one framed field experiment (Study 2). One study identifies motivation to respond without prejudice as a mediator of the effect of descriptive feedback about past choices on future selections of women and racial minorities. Another study shows that when women are overrepresented, the effect of descriptive feedback reverses in direction, increasing the subsequent selection of men (due to concerns about fairness), but this effect is significantly smaller in magnitude than the feedback effect produced when women are underrepresented. Practically, the effects of descriptive feedback were 45%–80% as large as simulating a strict quota requiring that at least one woman or racial minority be selected for a given opportunity, highlighting that descriptive feedback is a light-touch but potentially powerful intervention for promoting diversity. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01479 .

title: Human Performance at Solving 0-1 Knapsack Problems: Results from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
authors: Sumit Agarwal; Joel Goh; Wenlan Qian; Xin Zou
affiliations: NUS Business School, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119245; NUS Business School, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119245; and NUS Global Asia Institute, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119076; and NUS Institute of Operations Research and Analytics, National University of Singapore, Singapore 117602; NUS Business School, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119245; and NUS Institute of Real Estate and Urban Studies, National University of Singapore, Singapore; School of Business, Hong Kong Baptist University, Kowloon Tong, Hong Kong SAR
abstract: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. This paper reports the results of the first large-scale randomized controlled field experiment investigating this question, conducted in partnership with a global mobile gaming platform. A total of 100,000 different knapsack instances were predesigned for this study and randomly assigned to each player attempt at the knapsack problem. For our base-case analysis, there were 17,950,838 distinct player accounts who made a total of 150,284,195 submitted solution attempts. Contrary to expectations, players performed better on problems that were rated as more difficult by two traditional measures of knapsack difficulty (the Pearson correlation between value and weight vectors and Sahni complexity), but performed worse on problem instances that featured large optimality gaps from a suite of heuristic solution algorithms. These suggest that optimality gaps can serve as promising measures of human-perceived knapsack difficulty and potentially could be used to measure human-perceived problem difficulty for other types of discrete choice problems. We found evidence that players improved their performance with repeated attempts at the knapsack task overall, but less-experienced players of the mobile game improved more quickly than more-experienced players. Through the construction of a new measure of human-perceived difficulty rating for each knapsack instance, we found evidence that players who were assigned to instances with a higher difficulty rating in the past tended to perform better on future attempts. This paper was accepted by Manel Baucells, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: S. Agarwal’s research is supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore, under its Social Science and Humanities Research Thematic [Grant SSRC2024-SSHRTG-022] and the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. J. Goh’s research is supported by a Startup [Grant R-314-000-110-133] and a 2021 Humanities and Social Sciences Faculty Research Fellowship from the National University of Singapore. title: Connectors and Influencers
authors: Frédéric Moisan; Syngjoo Choi; Sanjeev Goyal
affiliations: Emlyon Business School, CNRS, Université Lumière Lyon 2, Université Jean Monnet Saint-Etienne, GATE, 69007 Lyon, France; Department of Economics, Seoul National University, Seoul 08826, Republic of Korea; Faculty of Economics, University of Cambridge, Cambridge CB3 9DD, United Kingdom
abstract: We study a setting in which personal acquisition of information is costly and maintaining personal contacts to share information socially is also costly. The theory predicts star networks, with small groups sustaining an active hub and large groups allowing in addition for an inactive hub equilibrium. Experiments with small (8 subjects) and large (50 subjects) groups show star-like networks throughout. In small groups, behavior matches the active hub prediction. In large groups, hubs are inactive or engage in activity far in excess of the active hub equilibrium depending on how much information subjects are given on their own and others’ earnings. The hub’s activity level shapes relative earnings of subjects and the overall performance of the group. This paper was accepted by Roberto Weber, behavioral economics and decision analysis. title: The Asymmetry in Responsible Investing Preferences and Beliefs
authors: Jacquelyn Humphrey; Shimon Kogan; Jacob S. Sagi; Laura T. Starks
affiliations: Business School, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Queensland 4072, Australia; Arison School of Business, Reichman University, Herzliya 4610101, Israel; Kenan-Flagler Business School, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina 27599; McCombs School of Business, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712
abstract: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior. Through a set of experiments, we examine whether such biases can be micro-founded via individuals’ preferences and belief formations. With respect to portfolio allocation decisions, we find that the responses to negative environmental and social externalities are several times larger in magnitude than their responses to comparable positive externalities, ceteris paribus. Negative externalities also modestly increase pessimism about future investment performance, whereas positive externalities have little discernible effect on beliefs. This asymmetry is pervasive across our sample, exhibits heterogeneity across individuals, and is comparable to or greater in magnitude than estimates observed in loss aversion analyses. These findings help rationalize several existing stylized empirical facts documented in the responsible investing literature and carry implications for the growing body of theoretical work modeling the role of nonpecuniary investor preferences in asset pricing. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. title: Decision Considerations Influencing Information Systems Modularity: A Multimethod Study of LEGO
authors: Stefan Henningsson; Ben Eaton; Lorenz Törmer; Suprateek Sarker
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School, Digitalization, Frederiksberg, Capital Region, Denmark; Copenhagen Business School, Department of Digitalization, Frederiksberg, 2000, Denmark; University of Virginia McIntire School of Commerce, Information Technology, Charlottesville, Virginia, United States
abstract: Abstract. The maturing of concepts such as microservices and open application programming interfaces (APIs) has radically increased the practicality of fine-grained modularization in Information Systems (IS) architecture. These are critical technical advancements, given the central role of modularity in the ability of IS to transform and meet future organizational needs efficiently. Nevertheless, reports from practice suggest that, when presented with new opportunities for modularization, organizations face multifaceted decision criteria and do not necessarily embrace new approaches as may be expected. While emergent IS literature observes that organizations’ decisions on modularity in IS may involve competing concerns, understanding of the considerations involved and how they influence such decisions remains limited. To examine these considerations, we intensively study the experience of LEGO, a global toy company. Specifically, we sequentially apply multiple methods consisting of an exploratory inductive analysis of LEGO’s approach to IS modularity decisions over 36 months, which then informs a crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of 31 episodes of LEGO’s situated decision-making on IS modularity. Through the analysis, we find the rationale for a purposeful choice between two forms of modularity that differ in granularity of decomposition, rather than a linear pursuit of maximizing decomposability in IS architecture. We bring to the fore a perspective of IS modularity as situated decisions reconciling competing demands in pursuit of the right type of modularity, in the right place to achieve the right effect. Our findings add nuance to modularity in the context of IS architecture and explain the complex causality of IS modularity decisions.

title: Online Review Generation in the Digital Age: A Meta-Analytic Study of Online Review Behavior
authors: Hong Hong; DaPeng Xu; Xiaoquan (Michael) Zhang
affiliations: Harbin Institute of Technology, School of Management, Harbin, China; Tsinghua University, Shenzhen International Graduate School, Shenzhen, China; Chinese University of Hong Kong, Decision Sciences and Managerial Economics, Shatin, N.T., CUHK Business School, Hong Kong
abstract: A large body of literature on online review generation has investigated various antecedents to online review characteristics. However, the mixed and even contradictory findings in this domain have hampered a clear understanding of consumers’ online review behavior for both researchers and practitioners, thereby complicating actionable strategies. To address this issue, we conduct a comprehensive meta-analysis of 154 independent samples from 152 empirical papers, synthesizing the relationships between 28 antecedent factors and 12 review features, which we categorize into rating-based (evaluative) and non-rating (expressive) dimensions. Our results indicate that rating attributes are dominantly driven by stable reviewer tendencies and market-level reputation cues, whereas non-rating features—such as text length and image inclusion—are primarily influenced by reviewer social embeddedness and platform engagement. Crucially, we identify that inconsistencies in prior literature can be explained by critical boundary conditions, including platform type (business-hosted vs. third-party), goods type (service vs. tangible), and cultural background (Asia vs. North America). By distinguishing between evaluative and expressive review components, our study reconciles mixed findings and uncovers underlying mechanisms such as expectation-based evaluation and self-presentation. The findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for empirical model specification and offer actionable insights for retailers and platforms to optimize reputation management and system design. Ultimately, our work offers a holistic framework for understanding online review behavior and proposes a rich agenda for future research in the digital marketplace.

title: From Design to Disclosure
authors: S Nageeb Ali; Andreas Kleiner; Kun Zhang
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University; University of Bonn; Auburn University and University of Queensland
abstract: Abstract We study the role of hard information in contractual and market settings in which the receiver can flexibly adjust allocations and transfers in response to the sender's disclosure. These settings include monopoly pricing, insurance contracting, and policy negotiations. Across these settings, the sender is worst off if she reveals her type completely because the receiver would then adjust the terms of trade to extract her surplus. Taking this feature as our central departure from the literature, we characterize the entire set of equilibrium payoffs in these disclosure games. We prove an equivalence result: a payoff profile can be approximated by an equilibrium of the disclosure game if and only if it can be achieved through information design. Thus, there exist equilibria in which the sender obtains approximately her commitment payoff.

title: Earnings Instability
authors: Peter Ganong; Pascal Noel; Christina Patterson; Joseph Vavra; Alexander Weinberg
affiliations: University of Chicago and National Bureau of Economic Research ,; University of Chicago ,
abstract: Abstract This paper uses high-frequency administrative data to show that most U.S. workers experience substantial month-to-month fluctuations in pay, even within ongoing employment relationships. Monthly earnings instability is pervasive but is masked in annual data. Moreover, this instability is unequally distributed: lower-income, hourly workers face more instability than higher-income, salaried workers. Firm-driven fluctuations in hours account for a large share of this instability. Monthly earnings instability, in turn, increases spending volatility and job separations. Short-term earnings risk is therefore a significant feature of the labor market and falls disproportionately on the most financially fragile workers.

title: Risk Assessment and Mitigation for International Multimodal Container Transport Networks Under Compound Flood and Tropical Cyclone Events
authors: Yifan Zhu; Mengqiao Xu; Ran Yan
affiliations: School of Economics and Management Dalian University of Technology Dalian Liaoning China; School of Civil and Environmental Engineering Nanyang Technological University Singapore Singapore
abstract: ABSTRACT International multimodal container transport networks (IMCTNs) play a critical role in supporting modern logistics systems and global trade, yet they are increasingly exposed to the risk of climate extremes, particularly compound flood and tropical cyclone (TC) events. The cross‐modal impact of such events and the resulting systemic risk to IMCTNs remain insufficiently understood. This study proposes a comprehensive methodological framework for assessing and mitigating risks in IMCTNs under compound flood‐TC events. By integrating multimodal transport and multisource data with climate hazard information, the framework enables probabilistic simulations of compound events ranging from frequent disturbances to rare extreme events and multi‐scale risk quantification at both the network and county levels. The framework proposes multiple component reinforcement strategies based on their criticality and disaster‐specific failure characteristics, thereby informing the design of targeted risk mitigation strategies. Applying the framework to a real‐world IMCTN in Mainland China, the results show that the relationship between network performance losses and events of different exceedance probabilities varies across probability ranges. Moreover, spatial heterogeneity is observed in that identical event probabilities lead to divergent losses across counties, which highlights the need for stratified monitoring frameworks for risk management. Finally, risk mitigation strategies accounting for both segment criticality and failure characteristics achieve superior effectiveness. The findings offer actionable guidance for risk mitigation in IMCTNs.

title: Correction to “Institutional Backsliding Under Liberal Democratic Backsliding: Central Bank Independence Reversal in Türkiye”
From Dysfunction to Socially Embedded Adaptation: A Constructive Pathway for Jealousy Toward Creativity in the Workplace
authors: Zhuofan Kan; Jin Nam Choi; Sun Young Sung
affiliations: School of Business Nanjing University Nanjing China; College of Business Administration Seoul National University Seoul South Korea
abstract: ABSTRACT Building on growing interest in social emotions in the workplace, this study examines the social cognitive pathway through which workplace jealousy can contribute to employee creativity. Drawing on social functional theory of emotion, we propose that workplace jealousy increases the focal person's recognition of others' ideas, which subsequently promotes creative performance. Furthermore, we hypothesize that political skills, such as social astuteness and networking ability, strengthen the indirect effect of workplace jealousy on employee creativity via the recognition of others' ideas. To test our hypotheses, we conducted three studies (Study 1: field data from 269 employees and their supervisors; Study 2: an online study based on the critical incident technique involving 276 working adults; and Study 3: a scenario‐based online experiment with 278 participants). Across the three studies, our analysis provides consistent patterns that workplace jealousy has a significant positive indirect effect on employee creativity via the recognition of others' ideas. Our analysis also shows that political skills strengthen this indirect relationship, although the results varied across the two dimensions. These results provide valuable theoretical insights into the constructive social functions of workplace jealousy toward creative processes, particularly for employees who are politically skilled.

title: Perspectives: A Tale of Three Plots: Advancing narrative theorising in organisation and management research
authors: Nele Langebraun; Bareerah Hafeez Hafeez Hoorani; Emmanuella Plakoyiannaki; Michael Gibbert; Joep Cornelissen
affiliations: HES-SO University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland; Institute of Marketing and Corporate Communication/ Università della Svizzera italiana, Lugano
abstract: Narrative theorising (rather than theorising based on constructs and models) is much called for in qualitative research in management and organisation studies. Despite this, how to emplot, i.e. the process of configuring fragmented events into coherent and meaningful accounts with the objective of sensemaking and understanding remains underexplored. This Perspectives piece showcases recent exemplars illustrating how we can practice narrative theorising using three distinct styles: historical, metaphorical, and discursive narratives. Since narrative theorising is commonly observed in single-case studies, we begin our exploration by drawing on six such articles published in Organization Studies to demonstrate how these styles foreground the temporal evolution of phenomena, bridge between multiple divergent accounts, or highlight conflicts between competing discourses to construct theoretical accounts and understanding. We illustrate each style in terms of its distinctive form, set of paradigmatic assumptions, analytical moves, and intended aims, with the overall aim of advancing the potential of narrative theorising in organisation and management research.

title: Constituting Technological Stigma: The Oscillating Stigmatization of Internal Combustion Engine Scooters
authors: I-lun Tsai; Ru-Mei Hsieh
abstract: Technologies can themselves become objects of stigmatization, rather than merely serving as vehicles through which stigma is directed at associated individuals or organizations. As technologies evolve, shifts in their benefits and harms may alter the grounds for stigma. Yet it remains unclear how these shifts shape stigma trajectories. We examine this issue through a longitudinal qualitative study of the stigmatization of internal combustion engine (ICE) scooters in Taiwan (2009–2021), a case in which a proposal to phase them out in favor of electric scooters was later withdrawn. We show how stigmatizing and stigmatized audiences, evolving technologies, and infrastructures co-constitute evaluative conditions that shape which attributes and consequences acquire discrediting significance. Stigma first attached to legacy ICE models and then spread to all ICE scooters. Its scope later narrowed as upgraded variants regained acceptance, although legacy models remained discredited. This oscillating trajectory unfolds through three mechanisms: constituting a graded technological order, polarizing this order, and reconstituting technological normality. Our model thus extends audience-centered accounts by explaining how human and nonhuman elements jointly shape the trajectory and scope of technology stigma.

title: Temporal Intuition and Organization Studies: Surfacing Intangible Time from a Sea Kayak
authors: Tor Hernes
abstract: Scholarship on organisational temporality has yet to fully take into account intangible time, defined in this essay as the creative connecting of fragmented temporal experiences through ‘temporal intuition’. This essay argues for a stronger attention to temporal intuition to enrich current understandings of temporal forms in organization studies. Inspired by Bergson’s work on lived temporal experience, it reports from the author’s direct experience of time during a 15-day solo sea-kayaking journey from Copenhagen to Oslo in August 2025. It shows how the experience of paddling in challenging weather and sea conditions required continued reliance on intuition to connect the multiple and dispersed temporal experiences encountered during the trip. Retrospective reflection on this experience has yielded three forms of temporal experience that can inspire further temporal theorizing: immanent events, inchoate rhythm, and contemporaneous flows. The essay concludes with suggestions on how to give temporal intuition a voice in organization studies by developing empirical, methodological and analytical aspects, thereby bringing intangible time from obscurity.

title: Partner selection in project-based software development: the roles of performance, collaboration experience and network governance
authors: Yingchao Lan; Tingting Yan; Brett Massimino
affiliations: University of Nebraska-Lincoln , , ,; Texas Tech University , , ,; Virginia Commonwealth University , , ,
abstract: Purpose This study examines supplier selection in project-based software development, where buyers rely on external developers for specialized capabilities while facing substantial safeguarding risks. Adopting a network-governance perspective, we investigate how network overlap – the extent to which a publisher and developer share common partners – moderates the relationships between developer performance, prior collaboration experience and selection outcomes. Design/methodology/approach Using a longitudinal dataset from the electronic video game industry (7,583 products, 4,322 unique developers and 3,016 unique publishers, over 16 years), we model developer selection using a conditional logit framework. Findings Developers with stronger historical product performance, confidentiality performance and greater prior collaboration experience are more likely to be selected. Network overlap substitutes for prior collaboration experience while strengthening the association between confidentiality performance and selection likelihood, highlighting the contingent role of network governance in partner selection decisions in project-based software development. Originality/value This study advances supplier-selection research by examining observed partner selection in project-based software development. It integrates firm-level indicators, dyadic experience and network overlap, showing that network governance can substitute for prior collaboration while complementing confidentiality performance.

title: CEOs’ job-hopping experience and supply chain relationships: insights from the attention-based view
authors: Fujuan Zhang; Yang Huang; Fangzhou Song; Yongjia Lin; Shuiquan Jiang
affiliations: School of Economics, Sichuan University , ,; Macau University of Science and Technology The Institute for Sustainable Development, , ,; School of Business, Macau University of Science and Technology , ,; School of Accounting, Chongqing Technology and Business University , ,
abstract: Purpose Drawing on the attention-based view, this study examines how CEOs’ job-hopping experience shapes supply chain relationships through managerial attention to supplier search and market expansion, and how CEOs’ R&D and production-line experience moderate these effects. Design/methodology/approach Using Chinese A-share listed firms from 2012 to 2024, this study hand-codes CEOs’ job-hopping experience from resumes and measures supplier and customer concentration based on disclosed top-five trading partner shares. We use fixed-effects models, mechanism and moderation tests and a series of robustness and endogeneity analyses. Findings Firms led by CEOs with more job-hopping experience exhibit higher supplier and customer concentration. Upstream, CEOs devote less attention to alternative supplier search, reflected in fewer tender projects and lower procurement-related recruitment, concentrating purchases among established suppliers. Downstream, CEOs give lower priority to market expansion, reflected in lower advertising expenditure and sales- and marketing-related recruitment, concentrating sales among established customers. CEOs’ R&D experience strengthens the supplier-side association, whereas their production-line experience strengthens the customer-side association. Both associations are stronger in non-state-owned firms and those facing greater performance pressure or higher capital intensity, while board production-line experience weakens the customer-side association. Originality/value This study extends supply chain relationship research beyond transactional and firm-level determinants by highlighting CEO career history as an explanation for firms’ different purchasing and sales patterns across trading partners. We extend the attention-based view by showing how experiences accumulated across organizational boundaries shape managerial attention, adding a historical dimension to managerial priorities. By linking managerial attention to observable supplier search and customer development activities, we clarify how CEO career history translates into supply chain relationship management and how prior functional experience shapes this process.

title: The Impacts of Host Culture Heterogeneity on Learning from Success Versus Failure in Foreign Direct Investments
authors: Yuping Zeng; Sangcheol Song; Soonkyoo Choe
affiliations: Southern Illinois University Edwardsville; Saint Joseph's University; Yonsei University
abstract: Abstract This study examines the differentiated influences of host culture heterogeneity on the learning outcomes of multinational enterprises' (MNEs) success and failure experiences in foreign direct investments (FDI). We posit that host culture heterogeneity among prior successful FDIs reduces the beneficial effect of an MNE's success experience on a subsequent FDI, particularly when the cultural differences between the subsequent FDI and the MNE's prior successes are significant. In contrast, host culture heterogeneity among prior failed FDIs enhances the learning benefits of failure experience, and this effect is more pronounced when the subsequent FDI is culturally distant from the prior failures. Using FDI data of South Korean MNEs between 1990 and 2016, we find support for our hypotheses, demonstrating that host culture heterogeneity has divergent impacts on the learning outcomes of MNEs' success versus failure FDI experiences. This study enhances our understanding of the conditions under which host culture heterogeneity may weaken or strengthen the learning benefits of an MNE's FDI experience.

title: Place Matters: A Dynamic Multilevel Perspective on Stigma Management in French Elderly Care
authors: Claire Le Breton; Frédéric Bally; Albane Grandazzi; Hélène Picard
affiliations: Grenoble Ecole de Management; KEDGE Business School
abstract: Abstract This article interrogates how ‘place’ contributes to managing stigma and its associated multilevel processes. In doing so, it addresses a literature that often treats stigma as a static attribute, overlooking the spatial and material dynamics of managing it. Drawing on a 2.5‐year case study of Help@hom, a French national initiative aimed at restructuring elderly care, we examine how spatial and material arrangements actively shape stigma management processes. We identify three interrelated mechanisms – expanding , enclosing , and fragmenting – through which Help@hom reconfigures the meanings, locations, and materialities of care. Building on these mechanisms, we theorize place as producing, sustaining, and distributing the dynamics of stigma management: place produces stigma management strategies rather than merely providing their setting, sustains stigma by relocating rather than dissolving it, and distributes it across organizational, occupational, and individual levels. Our study demonstrates that place is constitutive of stigma management, shaping how organizations enact and experience multilevel stigma processes, and that spatial and material interventions can produce unexpected cross‐level consequences. In doing so, it advances recent efforts to conceptualize stigma as relational, dynamic, and systemic, and offers a more integrated understanding of how organizations navigate complex stigma management landscapes.

title: May I Have Your Attention, Please? Debating the Ontology of Attention in Organizational Research
authors: Paolo Aversa; Christopher Wickert
affiliations: King's Business School, King's College London; School of Business and Economics Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
abstract: Abstract Few constructs in management research have proved as generative as organizational attention, and few have been left so largely unexamined at their core. This Point‐Counterpoint debate brings a dormant question into the open: what exactly is attention? The Point argues for an ontological reorientation of the Attention‐Based View from attention quantity to attention quality, reconceptualizing attention as a set of sociomaterial practices of attending that are crescive and differentiated rather than limited and homogeneous. One Counterpoint defends the ontological integrity of attention as scarce, selective, and situated, warning that a crescive ontology dissolves the very constraint from which attention derives its explanatory power. The other Counterpoint charts an expansive third way, tracing the contested assumptions to Herbert Simon's legacy and proposing to broaden the Attention‐Based View towards competition, thicker situations, and possible attentional abundance. In this introduction to the debate, we present the three positions and reflect on what their disagreement teaches us about ontological disputes in management theory more generally. We distil three tests – of phenomena, of explanation, and of genealogy – that scholars can apply when deciding whether a construct's ontology deserves revision, defence, or expansion.

title: From Managerial to Relational Epistemologies: Decolonizing Sustainability Education
authors: Subhabrata Bobby Banerjee
affiliations: Bayes Business School City St George's, University of London London UK
abstract: Abstract In this paper, I critically interrogate the epistemic foundations of sustainability education in business schools in the context of escalating climate crises. I argue that business education is complicit in the production and perpetuation of planetary destruction by privileging market‐based, growth‐driven rationalities while simultaneously co‐opting sustainability discourses to reinforce capitalist accumulation. These dominant managerialist regimes are epistemically resistant to the transformations required for sustainability and climate justice. Drawing on insights from decolonial scholarship and critical pedagogy, I explore the (im)possibilities of epistemic transformations that are needed for a more meaningful engagement with sustainability. I argue that such a transformation requires a shift from managerial to relational epistemologies—ways of knowing that emerge through relationships rather than detached observation of isolated, independent entities. Sustainability, from a relational epistemological perspective, cannot be divorced from social and environmental justice and must also confront power dynamics that drive inequality, neocolonialism and the exploitation of marginalized communities. I propose a radical reimagining of sustainability education—one that historicizes, denaturalizes and problematizes sustainability while prioritizing climate justice, relational ethics and pluriversal futures.

title:
The entrepreneur as ecosystem architect: Economic foundations for strategic entrepreneurship in the age of
                    <scp>AI</scp>
authors: David J. Teece
affiliations: Graduate School University of California, Berkeley Berkeley California USA; Berkeley Research Group Emeryville California USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper develops an alternative foundation for understanding strategic entrepreneurship in the age of artificial intelligence (AI) by joining entrepreneurship research with the profiting from innovation model and the dynamic capabilities framework. It argues that the economic function of the entrepreneur is increasingly that of an ecosystem architect, exercising judgment under uncertainty to orchestrate complementary assets and capabilities across organizational boundaries. AI dramatically lowers the cost of building software thereby lowering product development costs but may raise the barriers to scaling and sustaining competitive advantage. Value capture depends not simply on innovation, but on a compelling value proposition and access to and control over critical complementary assets, architectural control points, and shifting ecosystem bottlenecks. The paper emphasizes that entrepreneurial success requires dynamic capabilities and human judgment to configure and reconfigure ecosystems as technologies and competitive conditions evolve. Managerial Summary AI makes it easier to start a business as it lowers the cost of software development; but building a durable competitive advantage still requires more than a good product or technology. It requires a compelling value proposition to the customer and participation in ecosystems first as tenant and later as anchor. Accordingly, entrepreneurs need to become sophisticated ecosystem players and aspire to be architects, coordinating partners, platforms, data, technology, capital, and other capabilities they may not own. They should identify early which complementary assets are critical to creating and capturing value, understand where control and bottlenecks lie in their ecosystem, and continually reassess these as technology and competition change. AI can help small teams move faster and operate at greater scale, but it does not replace human judgment. Successful entrepreneurs must combine AI with strong ecosystem relationships, domain expertise, governance, and the ability to adapt as their businesses scale.

title: The old lady of economic history: 100 years of the Economic History Review
authors: Martina Cioni; Giovanni Federico; Michelangelo Vasta
affiliations: Department of Economics and Statistics University of Siena Siena Italy; Social Sciences Division New York University, Abu Dhabi, UAE and CEPR; Department of Economics and Statistics University of Siena, Siena, Italy, and CEPR
abstract: Abstract This article traces the evolution of the Economic History Review over its first century and places it within the broader transformation of economic history as a discipline. Drawing on a new database covering 2761 articles published in the journal between 1927 and 2025 by 2011 authors from 571 institutions in 50 countries, it analyses changes in editorial leadership, research topics, historical periods, geographical coverage, methods, authorship, and citation patterns. The findings suggest that the journal evolved from a predominantly UK outlet into one of the leading international journals in economic history. Over time, it converged towards the model of the major international field journals, with citation networks revealing a shift from stronger links with history to closer connections with economics. At the same time, however, the journal retained a distinctive profile, preserving a more historical orientation than the leading American journals. The article also documents a marked process of internationalization, reflected in both the geographical scope of published research and the growing presence of scholars from continental Europe. Finally, citation analysis shows that articles addressing long‐run and geographically comparative questions achieve the highest scholarly impact.

title: Partisan Banks and Creditor Coordination Within Loan Syndicates
authors: Robert M. Bushman; Sang Woo Sohn; Jianxin (Donny) Zhao
affiliations: University of North Carolina; City University of Hong Kong; Emory University
abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate how firm‐level partisanship influences interactions between banks in the syndicated loan market. Because politically divergent banks hold conflicting perceptions of economic conditions, ideological distance between banks impedes consensus and elevates expected coordination costs. We find that greater political distance between a lead arranger and a participant reduces the participant's likelihood of joining a syndicate and lowers its retained loan share relative to the lead. The relation between political distance and loan share differences intensifies during periods of high national political polarization. Moreover, greater political diversity within a syndicate is associated with less restrictive loan covenants and higher interest spreads, reflecting a trade‐off where lenders sacrifice contingent control to avoid costly renegotiation gridlock. Validating our disagreement mechanism, we show that following presidential elections, banks politically misaligned with the incoming administration issue significantly more pessimistic macroeconomic forecasts than aligned banks.

title: The Impact of Mandatory Audit Firm Rotation on Competitive Pricing Strategies for New Audit Engagements: Evidence From the European Union
authors: Ditmir Sufaj; Simon Dekeyser; Marleen Willekens
affiliations: KU Leuven Leuven Belgium
abstract: ABSTRACT Mandatory audit firm rotation was introduced in the European Union (EU), in part, to make the audit market more dynamic by bringing audit engagements to market more frequently. However, it creates a countervailing economic force: By limiting the duration of auditor–client relationships, mandatory rotation shortens the period over which auditors can recoup first‐year fee discounts through fees earned in subsequent years. Consistent with this argument, we find that first‐year fee discounts decline substantially after mandatory firm rotation took effect in the EU, particularly in countries with stricter limits on auditor tenure. Thus, greater opportunities to compete for new engagements do not necessarily translate into greater first‐year fee discounts. Our findings highlight that regulators should consider not only how frequently audit engagements are brought to market but also how limits on auditor tenure shape the pricing incentives associated with competing for new clients.
